moments.title: Silent Spring published
moments.body: Carson's book documents the ecological effects of synthetic pesticides. Chemical industry attacks the author and the science.

quote.text: The history of life on earth has been a history of interaction between living things and their surroundings.

moments.takeaway: A single book triggered structural changes in US environmental policy.

moments.title: EPA established and first Earth Day
moments.body: The first Earth Day on 22 April 1970 draws 20 million Americans. The Environmental Protection Agency is established in December.
moments.takeaway: Political pressure crystallised new federal institutions within a decade of Carson's book.

moments.title: DDT banned for agricultural use
moments.body: The agency bans most agricultural uses of DDT, citing accumulating ecological evidence.
moments.takeaway: Specific regulatory action followed from a broader public-science conversation.

now.title: Chemical regulation today
now.body: REACH (EU 2007) and analogous frameworks regulate thousands of chemicals. New concerns include PFAS, microplastics and endocrine disruptors.
now.open_questions: How should risk be assessed for chemicals in low-dose chronic exposure mixtures?

items.reflection: Environmental policy in the 20th century repeatedly hinged on writers and scientists able to translate evidence to public audiences.

moments.title: Molina and Rowland predict ozone loss
moments.who: Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland, UC Irvine
moments.body:
The pair publish a Nature paper arguing chlorofluorocarbons could destroy stratospheric ozone.

They win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1995 (with Paul Crutzen).
moments.takeaway: A theoretical prediction made years before instrumental confirmation.

moments.title: Antarctic ozone hole reported
moments.body: British Antarctic Survey scientists at Halley Bay publish data showing severe seasonal ozone depletion over Antarctica.
moments.takeaway: Patient long-term ground observations identified what satellites had filtered out.

moments.title: Montreal Protocol signed
moments.body: An international agreement phases down ozone-depleting substances. The protocol is widely cited as a model of effective environmental governance.
moments.takeaway: International cooperation produced measurable atmospheric improvement.

now.title: Stratospheric ozone today
now.body: WMO/UNEP assessments project recovery to 1980 levels around 2040 outside polar regions and 2066 over Antarctica. Unauthorised CFC-11 emissions detected in 2018 were addressed by 2021.
now.open_questions: Will geoengineering proposals (stratospheric aerosol injection) interact with ozone recovery? How robust is global compliance?

items.reflection: A relatively focused atmospheric problem with substitutable inputs produced a treaty that worked. Climate change has neither feature.

moments.title: IPCC established
moments.body:
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change is created to assess climate science for policymakers.

The first Assessment Report (1990) summarises the evidence base.
moments.takeaway: An international scientific assessment body became central to climate policy.

moments.title: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change
moments.body: The convention establishes the framework for international climate negotiations, leading to Kyoto (1997) and Paris (2015).
moments.takeaway: Climate diplomacy operates on multi-decade negotiation timescales.

moments.title: Paris Agreement adopted
moments.body: Parties agree to hold warming below 2 C and pursue 1.5 C, with nationally determined contributions reviewed every five years.
moments.takeaway: A bottom-up architecture replaced the Kyoto top-down approach.

now.title: Climate policy today
now.body: Net-zero targets are now legislated in many jurisdictions. IPCC AR6 (2021-2023) concluded human influence on warming is unequivocal. Implementation gaps remain large.
now.open_questions: Can policy gaps close by 2030 to keep 1.5 C in reach? What roles will carbon removal and adaptation play?

items.reflection: Climate negotiations show how scientific consensus and political action can travel at very different speeds.

moments.title: IUCN founded
moments.who: International Union for Conservation of Nature
moments.body: Founded in Fontainebleau, IUCN compiles the Red List of Threatened Species from 1964 onwards.
moments.takeaway: Conservation governance began as an inter-state and NGO initiative.

moments.title: Convention on Biological Diversity
moments.body: The Convention on Biological Diversity opens for signature, committing parties to biodiversity conservation, sustainable use and equitable benefit-sharing.
moments.takeaway: Biodiversity and climate frameworks emerged from the same political moment.

moments.title: Global Biodiversity Framework
moments.body: Parties agree to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030 ('30x30').
moments.takeaway: Quantitative biodiversity targets joined climate-style numerical pledges.

now.title: Biodiversity today
now.body: Living Planet Index and IUCN Red List both indicate continuing declines. Major drivers include land-use change, climate change, pollution and invasive species.
now.open_questions: How can biodiversity finance scale to delivery? What metrics best track ecosystem function rather than species counts alone?

items.reflection: Biodiversity policy has historically received less attention than climate; the two are increasingly treated as joined problems.

moments.title: Haeckel coins 'ecology'
moments.body: In 'Generelle Morphologie der Organismen', Haeckel coins 'Oecologie' from Greek 'oikos' (household) and 'logos' (study). He defines it as the study of the relationships between organisms and their environment. Haeckel was a fierce evolutionist and Darwin populariser, though some of his later social-Darwinist writing has not aged well.
moments.takeaway: A discipline's name preceded its content by decades. 'Ecology' existed before there were ecologists.

moments.title: Tansley defines the ecosystem
moments.body: Tansley's paper 'The Use and Abuse of Vegetational Concepts and Terms' (Ecology, 1935) coins 'ecosystem' as a unit including organisms and their physical environment as 'one physical system'. He explicitly objects to vitalistic 'organismic' framings of plant communities.
moments.takeaway: The ecosystem concept made ecology quantifiable. Energy, matter and information could flow through a defined unit.

moments.title: Lindeman's trophic-dynamic ecology
moments.body: Lindeman's paper on Cedar Bog Lake quantifies energy flow through trophic levels — producers, herbivores, carnivores — and introduces ecological efficiency. He dies at 27, before the paper appears posthumously and reshapes ecology.
moments.takeaway: The basic energy-flow model of ecosystems was set out in a single posthumous paper.

now.title: Ecosystem science today
now.body: Ecosystem services frameworks (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, 2005) and natural capital accounting (UK Dasgupta Review, 2021) extend Tansley's ecosystem to policy and economics. Earth system science (IGBP, 1987) treats the whole planet as a single biogeochemical system.
now.open_questions: Can ecosystem-services valuation prevent natural-capital depletion or does monetisation enable it?

items.reflection: Tansley named the ecosystem partly to combat the South African statesman Jan Smuts' holistic 'holism'. The intellectual battle over whether nature is 'mechanism' or 'organism' was decided when ecology became measurable.

moments.title: Malthus's Essay on Population
moments.body: An Essay on the Principle of Population argues population tends to grow geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically, leading inevitably to checks (war, famine, disease, moral restraint). The Essay shapes Darwin's reading of competition and Victorian poor-law debates alike.
moments.takeaway: A clergyman's economic-demographic argument from 1798 reframed the relationship between population, resources and ecology for two centuries.

moments.title: The Population Bomb
moments.body: Ehrlich's bestseller predicts mass starvation in the 1970s-80s. The Green Revolution (Norman Borlaug, 1960s — Nobel Peace Prize 1970) significantly delays the predicted famines through high-yield wheat and rice. Ehrlich's specific timeline was wrong; the underlying resource concerns recurred in different forms.
moments.takeaway: Neo-Malthusian predictions of the late 1960s did not arrive on schedule. The reasons (agricultural innovation, falling birth rates) matter.

now.title: Population today
now.body: World population: ~8 billion (2022, UN estimate). Projected to peak at ~10.4 billion in 2086 then decline. Fertility is now below replacement in most of Europe, East Asia and parts of the Americas. The 21st-century challenge has flipped from population growth to population decline and ageing in many regions.
now.open_questions: Can food systems support 10 billion people sustainably? Demand-side change (diet, waste) may matter more than supply-side.

items.reflection: Malthus's argument is rarely correct in its details but recurs in environmental thought (Club of Rome 'Limits to Growth' 1972, planetary boundaries 2009). Whether each generation is 'Malthus was wrong' or 'Malthus was just early' depends on the time horizon.

moments.title: Yosemite Grant signed
moments.body: In the middle of the Civil War, Lincoln signs the Yosemite Grant on 30 June 1864, ceding Yosemite Valley and Mariposa Grove to California for preservation. It's the first federal protection of land for public preservation purposes.
moments.takeaway: The world's first protected park-for-preservation predates the National Park concept and was signed during a war.

moments.title: Yellowstone, first national park
moments.body: Yellowstone National Park is established on 1 March 1872 — the first national park in the modern sense, federally administered. Indigenous Sheep Eater and other peoples are displaced from the land. The 'wilderness' the parks preserve is a curated absence of certain humans.
moments.takeaway: National parks created a model of protected wilderness, with significant costs for indigenous communities.

moments.title: Sierra Club founded
moments.who: John Muir and others, San Francisco
moments.body: Muir co-founds the Sierra Club to protect the Sierra Nevada. His relentless writing and lobbying (and his 1903 camping trip with Theodore Roosevelt) shape US conservation. Roosevelt establishes 5 national parks, 18 national monuments, 51 federal bird reserves and 150 national forests during his presidency (1901-1909).
moments.takeaway: American conservation became politics through specific friendships and writings, not as inevitable consequence of population pressure.

now.title: Protected areas today
now.body: ~17% of land and ~8% of oceans are protected globally (2024). The Kunming-Montreal '30x30' target aims for 30% by 2030. Conflicts over indigenous rights, tourism, and ecological function continue. The Sierra Club has reckoned publicly with Muir's racist statements about Black people and indigenous Americans (2020 statement by then-Executive Director Michael Brune).
now.open_questions: Can 'fortress conservation' (people-free parks) coexist with indigenous-led conservation models, which empirically often produce better outcomes?

items.reflection: Muir saw wilderness as cathedral. Aldo Leopold (Sand County Almanac, 1949) added the 'land ethic'. Both inherit and reshape American settler relationships with land that displaced its original inhabitants.

moments.title: Eunice Foote measures CO₂ heating
moments.body: Foote's experiments, presented at the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1856 (read by a man because women could not present), show that CO₂ absorbs more solar heat than common air. She speculates that varying atmospheric CO₂ would change Earth's temperature.
moments.takeaway: The greenhouse effect was experimentally demonstrated by a woman three years before Tyndall — and was forgotten.

moments.title: Tyndall measures infrared absorption
moments.body: Tyndall demonstrates that water vapour and CO₂ absorb infrared radiation, identifying the greenhouse mechanism. His more thorough quantitative work establishes the field; Foote's work is rediscovered only in 2010.
moments.takeaway: Two independent demonstrations of the greenhouse effect within three years; the better-funded man's career and credit endured.

moments.title: Arrhenius's CO₂-doubling calculation
moments.body: Arrhenius calculates that doubling atmospheric CO₂ would warm the Earth by ~5-6 °C (modern climate sensitivity: ~3 °C). He spends most of the next year doing the calculations by hand, motivated partly by the cold of a Stockholm winter and recent divorce. He considers the warming a positive future development.
moments.takeaway: The basic mathematics of CO₂-driven climate change was done by 1896. The atmosphere has continued to behave roughly as Arrhenius predicted.

now.title: Climate science today
now.body: Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from ~280 ppm (pre-industrial) to 422 ppm (2024). Global mean temperature is ~1.2 °C above pre-industrial. The mechanism Tyndall and Arrhenius identified has not changed; the magnitude is now well-measured. Climate sensitivity estimates have narrowed to ~2.5-4 °C (IPCC AR6).
now.open_questions: Where exactly does climate sensitivity sit within the range? Cloud feedbacks remain the biggest uncertainty.

items.reflection: Eunice Foote's 1856 paper was found in a digitised AAAS Proceedings in 2010. The history of science is not fixed; it is constantly rewritten by archive work.

moments.title: Keeling starts measuring
moments.who: Charles David Keeling, Scripps Institution of Oceanography
moments.body: Keeling begins continuous atmospheric CO₂ measurements at Mauna Loa Observatory in March 1958 (~315 ppm) and at the South Pole. He fights repeatedly for funding to continue. The 'Keeling Curve' becomes the canonical visualisation of climate change.
moments.takeaway: A single scientist's stubborn insistence on long-term measurement produced the most-cited dataset in environmental science.

moments.title: James Hansen testifies
moments.body: On 23 June 1988, in 38 °C heat in Washington DC, Hansen tells the US Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources that 'global warming is now sufficiently large that we can ascribe with a high degree of confidence a cause-and-effect relationship to the greenhouse effect.' The IPCC is established later that year.

quote.text: It is time to stop waffling so much and say the evidence is pretty strong that the greenhouse effect is here.

moments.takeaway: A scientist's congressional testimony, on a record-hot day, made climate change a political issue.

now.title: CO₂ monitoring today
now.body: Atmospheric CO₂ exceeded 420 ppm in 2023 — the highest in at least 800,000 years (ice cores) and likely in millions of years. The Keeling Curve continues, run by Keeling's son Ralph after his father's death (2005). Methane and nitrous oxide are also closely monitored. Satellite missions (OCO-2, GOSAT, MethaneSAT) extend coverage.
now.open_questions: Can atmospheric CO₂ stabilise this century? Net-zero pledges imply yes; actual emissions trajectories suggest no.

items.reflection: Keeling told a 1969 hearing that CO₂ was rising and could change climate. Hansen testified again. Bill McKibben wrote 'The End of Nature' (1989). Greta Thunberg began the school strikes (2018). Each generation makes climate change more visible; the curve continues.

moments.title: Stockholm Conference
moments.body: The UN Conference on the Human Environment, 5-16 June 1972, is the first major UN conference on international environmental issues. 113 nations attend. The Stockholm Declaration (26 principles) and an action plan emerge. UNEP (UN Environment Programme) is created, headquartered in Nairobi.
moments.takeaway: The international environmental governance architecture in active use today began with one conference in Sweden in 1972.

now.title: International environmental governance today
now.body: UNEP coordinates global environmental policy, hosts MEAs (Multilateral Environmental Agreements), and produces the annual Emissions Gap Report. The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (1992), CBD (1992), UNCCD (1994) and successors all trace lineage to Stockholm.
now.open_questions: Can fragmented MEAs evolve into coherent Earth system governance? IPBES (biodiversity, 2012) and other panels increasingly try to link them.

items.reflection: Indira Gandhi's Stockholm speech argued: 'Are not poverty and need the greatest polluters?' The development-vs-environment tension framed at Stockholm runs through every subsequent COP and SDG negotiation.

moments.title: Our Common Future
moments.who: World Commission on Environment and Development, chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland (Norway)
moments.body: The Brundtland Report defines sustainable development as 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.' The phrase becomes the orthodox framing of environmental policy for the next forty years.

quote.text: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

moments.takeaway: A single sentence drafted by a UN commission framed the global development policy agenda for forty years.

now.title: Sustainable development today
now.body: The Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015) and Sustainable Development Goals (2015-2030, 17 goals, 169 targets) operationalised Brundtland. Critics argue 'sustainable development' is sufficiently elastic to mean nothing. Defenders argue it preserved environmental concerns through decades of growth-oriented politics.
now.open_questions: Are the SDGs on track for 2030? Implementation gaps are large; the UN's 2023 SDG Progress Report says only ~15% of targets are on track.

items.reflection: Brundtland was a paediatrician and Norway's first female Prime Minister. The most-quoted environmental policy phrase of the past 40 years came from a doctor running a country who was asked to chair a commission.

moments.title: Rio Earth Summit
moments.body: The UN Conference on Environment and Development, 3-14 June 1992, gathers 172 governments (108 heads of state). Outputs: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), Forest Principles, Rio Declaration, and Agenda 21 — a 350-page action plan for sustainable development at all governance levels.
moments.takeaway: Three of the core international environmental treaties operating today opened for signature at one conference in 1992.

now.title: Rio process today
now.body: COP (Conference of Parties) meetings for UNFCCC (annual, COP29 Baku 2024), CBD (biennial, COP16 Cali 2024), and UNCCD coordinate global environmental treaty implementation. Rio+20 (2012) launched the SDG process. Civil-society participation at COPs has grown; so have fossil-fuel lobbyist registrations.
now.open_questions: Can the COP process deliver implementation at the pace required by the science?

items.reflection: Severn Cullis-Suzuki, age 12, addressed Rio: 'If you don't know how to fix it, please stop breaking it.' Thirty years later, Greta Thunberg gave similar speeches to similar audiences. Inter-generational ethics has become a permanent feature of climate diplomacy.

moments.title: Kyoto Protocol adopted
moments.body: The Kyoto Protocol binds developed (Annex I) countries to specific emissions reductions averaging ~5% below 1990 levels by 2008-2012. It introduces emissions trading, the Clean Development Mechanism, and Joint Implementation. The US signs but never ratifies (rejected by the Senate 95-0 in the Byrd-Hagel resolution, 1997).
moments.takeaway: The first binding international climate treaty was undermined by US non-ratification, then by China and India having no targets despite rapid growth.

now.title: Climate treaties today
now.body: Kyoto's binding top-down architecture gave way to Paris's nationally determined contributions (2015) — pledges by each country, reviewed every five years. The first Global Stocktake (Dubai COP28, 2023) explicitly mentioned 'transitioning away from fossil fuels' for the first time in 30 years of UNFCCC negotiations.
now.open_questions: Are bottom-up pledges adequate without binding enforcement?

items.reflection: The legal architecture of climate treaties matters less than the underlying political consensus. Kyoto was legally binding and largely ignored. Paris is non-binding and has driven more action — because more major emitters have signed up.

moments.title: Six IPCC Assessment cycles
moments.body: AR1 (1990): warming 'could be largely due to natural variability'. AR2 (1995): 'discernible human influence'. AR3 (2001): 'most of the warming over the last 50 years is likely to have been due to'. AR4 (2007): 'very likely'. AR5 (2013-14): 'extremely likely'. AR6 (2021-23): 'unequivocal' that human influence has warmed the climate.
moments.takeaway: The IPCC's escalating certainty across 33 years tracks both improving science and the difficulty of conveying consensus to policymakers.

now.title: Climate assessment today
now.body: The IPCC's AR7 cycle is underway (2024-2030). The Special Reports — SR1.5 (2018), SRCCL (2019, land), SROCC (2019, ocean and cryosphere) — proved increasingly influential. IPCC reports are now central inputs to COP negotiations.
now.open_questions: How does the IPCC handle accelerating non-linear changes (tipping points)? AR6 increased emphasis but more is needed.

items.reflection: The IPCC does not conduct research; it synthesises. Its statements are negotiated word by word in governmental approval sessions. The line between scientific summary and political compromise is real.

moments.title: Sustainable Development Goals adopted
moments.who: United Nations General Assembly, New York
moments.body: On 25 September 2015, all 193 UN member states adopt the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development with 17 SDGs and 169 targets. Goals span poverty, hunger, health, education, gender equality, water, energy, work, infrastructure, inequality, cities, consumption, climate, oceans, land, peace, partnerships.
moments.takeaway: A global agreement on what 'development' should mean now exists; whether implementation matches ambition is contested.

now.title: SDGs today
now.body: The 2023 SDG Summit reported only ~15% of targets on track; the rest stalled, stagnant or going backwards. COVID-19, food and energy crises, and conflict reversed progress on poverty and hunger. SDG financing gap: ~$4 trillion/year. The Pact for the Future (2024) sought to refocus.
now.open_questions: Can a post-2030 development framework learn from the SDGs' implementation gaps?

items.reflection: The SDGs replaced the Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015). MDGs had 8 goals; SDGs have 17. Whether breadth helps or dilutes accountability is the central design debate of global development.

moments.title: BioDiversity volume published
moments.who: E. O. Wilson (ed.), National Academy of Sciences
moments.body: The proceedings of the 1986 National Forum on BioDiversity, edited by Wilson, popularise the term 'biodiversity' and document rapid species loss. Wilson estimates 27,000 species lost per year in tropical forests. He goes on to propose the 'Half-Earth' project (2016) — protect half the planet for nature.
moments.takeaway: The very word 'biodiversity' was popularised in 1988. Until then, conservation talked about 'species' or 'wildlife'; the broader concept was newly named.

moments.title: Sixth mass extinction case
moments.who: Anthony Barnosky, Gerardo Ceballos, et al.
moments.body: A series of papers (Barnosky et al. 2011 Nature; Ceballos et al. 2015, 2017 PNAS) argue current extinction rates are 100-1000x background, comparable to the five previous mass extinctions. The IPBES Global Assessment (2019) estimates 1 million species threatened.
moments.takeaway: The 'sixth mass extinction' framing entered mainstream science in the 2010s — and is contested in detail (the rates are uncertain) but not in direction.

now.title: Biodiversity today
now.body: The Living Planet Index (WWF/ZSL) reports a 73% average decline in monitored wildlife populations since 1970. The IUCN Red List has assessed ~150,000 species; over 40,000 are threatened. The Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) commits to halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030.
now.open_questions: Are LPI's 73% headline figures statistically sound? The methodology has been critiqued; revisions are smaller but still negative.

items.reflection: Wilson predicted that conservation biology would become the dominant biological science of the 21st century — not for theoretical reasons but as triage. The discipline has not become dominant. The triage continues.

moments.title: Anthropocene proposed
moments.body: At a 2000 IGBP meeting, Crutzen interrupts to say 'No, we are in the Anthropocene!' (rather than the Holocene). The term — humans as a geological force — spreads rapidly. The Anthropocene Working Group spent 2009-2024 proposing a formal stratigraphic definition.
moments.takeaway: An off-the-cuff remark by a Nobel laureate launched the most influential geological-period concept of the 21st century.

moments.title: Planetary boundaries
moments.who: Johan Rockström and team, Stockholm Resilience Centre
moments.body: The 2009 Nature paper identifies nine processes critical to a stable Earth system (climate change, ocean acidification, ozone, biogeochemical flows, freshwater, land use, biodiversity, aerosols, novel entities) with quantitative 'safe operating space' boundaries. The 2023 update finds 6 of 9 boundaries crossed.
moments.takeaway: An attempt to quantify safe operating space for humanity gave policymakers a dashboard rather than a single climate target.

moments.title: Anthropocene rejected as formal epoch
moments.body: On 4 March 2024, the ICS subcommission votes against formalising the Anthropocene as a geological epoch starting ~1950. Geologists wanted a clear stratigraphic marker; the proposed Crawford Lake (Canada) marker failed to convince. The concept survives as informal usage.
moments.takeaway: A scientific term can be enormously influential in policy and culture without formal geological status.

now.title: Anthropocene today
now.body: The concept underlies Earth system science, planetary boundaries, the SDGs and most major environmental thinking. Whether 'humans' (in general) or specific economic systems (Capitalocene, Plantationocene) are the right actors is debated.
now.open_questions: If the Anthropocene is not a formal epoch, how should the geological community describe a planet altered by humans? An 'event' is the current proposal.

items.reflection: Crutzen won the 1995 Nobel for ozone-layer chemistry — and proposed solar radiation management (stratospheric aerosols) in 2006. The man who diagnosed the Anthropocene also proposed engineering it.

moments.title: Great Smog of London
moments.body: From 5-9 December 1952, an anticyclone traps coal smoke over London. Visibility drops to a few metres. ~4,000 excess deaths in the immediate event; modern estimates put total deaths at 10,000-12,000 over the following months. Cattle at Smithfield market suffocate.
moments.takeaway: A single weather event made urban coal-burning politically unsustainable. The Clean Air Act 1956 created smoke control areas.

moments.title: US Clean Air Act
moments.body: The 1970 Clean Air Act gives the EPA authority to set National Ambient Air Quality Standards. Lead is phased out from petrol (1973-86). Particulate matter standards (PM10, then PM2.5) are added later. Acid rain control (1990 amendments) succeeds via cap-and-trade.
moments.takeaway: US air pollution regulation through the 1970s-90s achieved measurable reductions in lead, SO₂ and NOₓ while the economy grew.

now.title: Air pollution today
now.body: WHO estimates 7 million premature deaths annually from air pollution. PM2.5 is the major killer. London's Ultra Low Emission Zone (2019, expanded 2023) has measurably improved NO₂. China's massive coal-burning has caused major air-quality crises; Beijing's APEC Blue (2014) showed both the problem and a response.
now.open_questions: Will indoor air quality (cooking fuels in low-income countries; wildfire smoke in high-income countries) be tackled with the same urgency as outdoor?

items.reflection: The 1952 smog killed roughly as many Britons as the Blitz in a single week. It took four years for parliament to pass legislation. Environmental policy moves at parliamentary, not biological, speeds.

moments.title: Snow maps the Broad Street pump
moments.body: Snow's map of cholera deaths in Soho shows a cluster around the Broad Street water pump. He persuades the local board of guardians to remove the pump handle on 8 September 1854; the outbreak subsides. The pump was contaminated by a nearby leaking cesspit.
moments.takeaway: Modern epidemiology — and the case for safe drinking water — was made by one doctor with a map.

now.title: Water and health today
now.body: 2.2 billion people lack safely managed drinking water (WHO/UNICEF 2023). The UN Sustainable Development Goal 6 targets universal access by 2030. The 2014 Flint, Michigan water crisis (lead contamination from corrosion after a cost-cutting source switch) showed that water safety in wealthy countries is not guaranteed either.
now.open_questions: How will climate-driven water stress affect access? Cape Town's 'Day Zero' (2018) was averted but the model recurs.

items.reflection: The Broad Street pump replica still stands in Soho with a handle removed, near a pub named the John Snow. Public health interventions can be remarkably specific — pull a handle, save thousands of lives.

moments.title: Chernobyl explosion
moments.body: At 01:23:40 on 26 April 1986, Reactor 4 of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant explodes during a safety test, releasing ~400 times the radioactivity of Hiroshima. 31 immediate deaths. Estimates of total long-term deaths range from ~4,000 (WHO 2005) to >90,000 (TORCH 2006). The 30-km exclusion zone remains in force.
moments.takeaway: The most consequential civilian nuclear accident reshaped public attitudes to nuclear energy for decades and accelerated Soviet glasnost.

moments.title: Fukushima Daiichi
moments.body: On 11 March 2011, the Tōhoku earthquake (magnitude 9.0) and subsequent tsunami (up to 40m) overwhelm Fukushima Daiichi's defences. Three reactors melt down. ~150,000 evacuated. Direct radiation deaths: zero in the short term; the evacuation itself caused significant indirect deaths. Germany phases out nuclear power; Japan idles its fleet for years.
moments.takeaway: A second major nuclear accident reset global nuclear-power politics. Decades of climate-policy debate had to confront the nuclear question again.

now.title: Nuclear today
now.body: Nuclear provides ~10% of global electricity. New designs (small modular reactors, advanced reactors) seek to address safety and economics. France, Sweden, the UK and the US are extending reactor lifetimes. Japan is restarting reactors. Germany completed nuclear phase-out in 2023; it now imports more electricity, partly from coal.
now.open_questions: Can nuclear scale fast enough to contribute to net-zero by 2050? Construction time and capital cost are the central problems.

items.reflection: Wildlife has recolonised the Chernobyl exclusion zone in ways that suggest the absence of humans matters more for many species than radiation does. A grim natural experiment in rewilding.

moments.title: Bhopal gas disaster
moments.body: On the night of 2-3 December 1984, ~40 tonnes of methyl isocyanate gas leaks from the Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal. Conservative immediate deaths: ~2,259; conservative total: 15,000+. ~500,000 exposed. The site remains contaminated; groundwater is unsafe. Union Carbide paid $470 million in 1989 settlement. Warren Anderson (CEO) never faced trial in India.
moments.takeaway: The world's worst industrial accident produced a settlement of less than $1,000 per dead victim and an unprosecuted CEO.

now.title: Industrial chemical safety today
now.body: EU Seveso III Directive (2012) regulates major-hazard industrial facilities, named for the 1976 Italian dioxin leak. The US Risk Management Program (1990 Clean Air Act amendments) requires facility safety plans. Bhopal survivors and second-generation victims continue to seek justice; the site remains incompletely remediated.
now.open_questions: How can industrial-accident liability scale across borders? Multinationals can shield themselves through corporate structure.

items.reflection: Bhopal made 'environmental justice' a global concept, not merely a US one. The disaster's combination of poverty, regulation gaps and corporate impunity recurred at Marikana, Brumadinho, and many less-known sites.

moments.title: Exxon Valdez
moments.body: On 24 March 1989, the Exxon Valdez tanker runs aground on Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, Alaska, spilling 11 million gallons (~37,000 tonnes) of crude oil. Captain Joseph Hazelwood was below deck; the third mate was steering. Effects on sea otter, seal and seabird populations persisted for decades. Exxon paid ~$2 billion in clean-up and $507 million in punitive damages after a Supreme Court reduction from $5 billion.
moments.takeaway: The Oil Pollution Act 1990 required double-hulled tankers in US waters and reshaped maritime pollution liability.

moments.title: Deepwater Horizon
moments.body: On 20 April 2010, the Deepwater Horizon drilling rig in the Gulf of Mexico explodes; 11 workers die. 4.9 million barrels of oil flow into the Gulf over 87 days before the well is capped. BP paid ~$65 billion in clean-up, settlements and fines. The disaster reshaped offshore drilling regulation under the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management.
moments.takeaway: Deepwater drilling for the marginal barrel of oil produced the largest marine oil spill in history.

now.title: Marine pollution today
now.body: Oil spills have declined sharply since the 1990s (ITOPF data) due to double-hulled tankers, better salvage and routing. Plastic pollution (~14 million tonnes/year into oceans), eutrophication-driven dead zones, ghost fishing gear, and chronic shipping pollution now dominate. The Global Plastics Treaty (under negotiation 2022-2025) seeks systematic regulation.
now.open_questions: Can plastics production be capped, or only better managed? The treaty negotiations turn on this.

items.reflection: Exxon knew about climate change by the late 1970s (internal documents revealed by Inside Climate News 2015) but funded denial campaigns through the 1990s and 2000s. The same companies cause and conceal.

moments.title: Martha dies
moments.body: Martha, the last passenger pigeon, dies on 1 September 1914 at age ~29. The species had numbered in the billions in the early 19th century — possibly the most numerous bird ever — and was hunted to extinction within decades. Audubon described flocks 'darkening the air for days' in 1813.
moments.takeaway: The most numerous bird in North American history went extinct within a human lifetime, driven by industrial-scale hunting and habitat destruction.

moments.title: Northern white rhino's last male dies
moments.body: Sudan, the last male northern white rhino, dies on 19 March 2018. Only two females remain. The subspecies is functionally extinct. IVF efforts using preserved sperm and northern white rhino eggs are underway; the first embryos were created in 2019.
moments.takeaway: A subspecies can persist genetically (frozen cells) even after biological extinction. What 'extinction' means is becoming technically negotiable.

now.title: Extinction today
now.body: IUCN Red List recognises 900+ species as extinct since 1500. Recent vertebrate extinctions include the baiji (Yangtze river dolphin, declared functionally extinct 2006), the western black rhino (2011) and several frog species. De-extinction efforts (Colossal Biosciences working on mammoth, dodo, thylacine) are technologically real and ethically contested.
now.open_questions: Should de-extinction be pursued? Resources spent on resurrecting lost species cannot be spent on preserving extant ones.

items.reflection: Martha's body was packed in ice and sent to the Smithsonian, where she is on display. Her species' total population fell from billions to one. The largest population can vanish if every individual is killed.

moments.title: Chico Mendes assassinated
moments.body: Chico Mendes, rubber tapper and Amazon activist, is assassinated on 22 December 1988 by ranchers in Acre, Brazil. His murder draws international attention to Amazon deforestation. Brazil establishes extractive reserves named for him; INPE (the National Institute for Space Research) begins systematic deforestation monitoring via satellite (PRODES, 1988-).
moments.takeaway: Effective Amazon monitoring began with — and was partly motivated by — an assassinated activist's campaign.

moments.title: Brazil's deforestation falls 80%
moments.body: Under Lula's first term, Brazil reduces annual Amazon deforestation from 27,772 km² (2004) to 4,571 km² (2012) — an 80% drop — through PPCDAm enforcement, satellite monitoring, supply-chain agreements (Soy Moratorium 2006, Cattle Agreement 2009) and protected-area expansion.
moments.takeaway: Deforestation is policy-responsive. Where political will and tools coincide, large reductions are possible — and quickly reversible.

now.title: Amazon today
now.body: Deforestation surged under Bolsonaro (2019-22) and fell again under Lula (2023-). The forest is approaching tipping-point estimates: research suggests the Amazon could shift from carbon sink to carbon source through ~20-25% deforestation (currently ~17%). Indonesian peatland loss has slowed since 2016 due to moratoria.
now.open_questions: What deforestation threshold tips the Amazon to savanna? Recent research suggests it may already be a net carbon source in dry years.

items.reflection: The Amazon's policy history shows neither technological inevitability nor permanent doom. National political shifts move deforestation curves visibly within years. Agency matters.

moments.title: Bell Labs silicon solar cell
moments.who: Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller and Gerald Pearson, Bell Labs
moments.body: Bell Labs announces the first practical silicon photovoltaic cell on 25 April 1954 — 6% efficient. The first applications are powering remote telephone equipment. Early space applications (Vanguard 1 satellite, 1958) prove the technology in orbit. Costs remain prohibitively high for terrestrial use for decades.
moments.takeaway: Solar power was a laboratory novelty for 50 years, a space technology for 30, and a mainstream energy source for less than 20.

moments.title: First commercial wind farms
moments.body: The first major wind farms appear in California's Altamont Pass and Tehachapi (1980s) under tax-credit incentives. Denmark systematically supports cooperative ownership. By 2000 wind power is cost-competitive in good sites; by 2020 it's the cheapest electricity in most markets.
moments.takeaway: Persistent policy support and learning curves drove wind costs down by ~90% from the 1980s to today.

moments.title: UK legislates net-zero by 2050
moments.body: On 27 June 2019 the UK becomes the first G7 nation to legislate net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. By the early 2020s, most major economies have similar targets. The Climate Change Committee (Lord Deben/John Gummer) advises on the trajectory; the UK met its first three carbon budgets but is off-track for the fourth and fifth.
moments.takeaway: Net-zero pledges became legally binding mainstream policy in less than a decade after Paris.

now.title: Energy transition today
now.body: Solar PV is now the cheapest electricity ever recorded (~$0.02/kWh in best locations). 80% of new electricity capacity added globally in 2023 was renewable. Coal use is still rising globally (India, China) but peaking; EU coal use has fallen 75% since 1990. Batteries, electric vehicles, heat pumps and electrolysers complete the system.
now.open_questions: Can grid infrastructure, storage and permitting keep up with renewable deployment? Industrial decarbonisation and aviation remain hard.

items.reflection: The IEA spent two decades systematically under-projecting solar deployment, then over-corrected. Energy forecasts get the speed of change wrong in both directions; structural shifts are hard to predict.

moments.title: DuPont and 3M PFAS revelations
moments.body: Internal documents reveal DuPont and 3M knew of PFOA/PFOS health risks for decades but did not report them. Robert Bilott, a corporate lawyer turned plaintiff's attorney, sues DuPont over Parkersburg, West Virginia contamination — eventually settling for $671 million in 2017. The 'Dark Waters' (2019) film dramatises the case.
moments.takeaway: Chemicals that everyone now carries in their blood (PFAS are detected in ~99% of humans tested) were marketed for decades while the manufacturers knew of risks.

now.title: PFAS today
now.body: PFAS are a class of ~5,000+ 'forever chemicals' — extremely persistent fluorinated compounds. EU is moving to restrict all PFAS (proposal 2023, decision pending). US EPA set drinking water limits in 2024. They are used in non-stick cookware, waterproof clothing, firefighting foam, semiconductor manufacturing.
now.open_questions: Can PFAS be removed from water at scale? Treatment exists but is expensive. Replacement chemicals (GenX) raise similar concerns.

items.reflection: PFAS appear in the planetary boundaries framework under 'novel entities'. The 2023 update found this boundary 'transgressed'. The chemicals we synthesise faster than we can assess them are now a recognised planetary risk.

moments.title: First global mass bleaching
moments.body: The 1997-98 El Niño triggers the first known global-scale coral bleaching event. ~16% of world's reef coral dies. Subsequent global events: 2010, 2014-17 (longest on record, ~75% of reefs affected), 2023-24 (ongoing as of early 2024). Each event reduces resilience.
moments.takeaway: A global ecosystem can undergo mass mortality events at decade scales while industrial society remains barely aware.

now.title: Reefs today
now.body: The Great Barrier Reef has experienced six mass bleaching events (1998, 2002, 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024). UNESCO has been deciding whether to list it 'in danger'. Research on coral assisted evolution, larval seeding and shading are ongoing. Reef tourism remains economically significant but ecologically uncertain.
now.open_questions: Can reefs survive 1.5 C of warming? IPCC SR1.5 (2018) said 70-90% of warm-water corals would be lost at 1.5 C; 99% at 2 C.

items.reflection: The Great Barrier Reef is one of the few ecosystems visible from space. Its loss within the careers of the scientists who study it has reshaped marine biology into something closer to disaster medicine.

moments.title: Charles Moore finds the patch
moments.who: Charles Moore, Algalita Marine Research Foundation
moments.body: Moore, sailing through the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre after a yacht race, encounters extensive plastic debris in what becomes known as the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. His subsequent research (with Captain Curtis Ebbesmeyer) brings the concept of ocean plastic to public attention.
moments.takeaway: A subtropical ocean gyre had been concentrating plastic for decades before the wider public learned about it from one sailor's observation.

moments.title: Plastic found in Mariana Trench
moments.body: On a 10,927m dive into the Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep), Vescovo's submersible records video of a plastic bag and sweet wrappers at the deepest point of the ocean.
moments.takeaway: There is no part of the ocean unaffected by human plastic. The lowest point of the seabed is contaminated.

now.title: Ocean plastics today
now.body: ~14 million tonnes of plastic enter the oceans annually. Microplastics are found in clouds, rain, breast milk and the placenta. The UN Global Plastics Treaty has been negotiated since 2022 (INC sessions 1-5). The Ocean Cleanup, single-use plastic bans and producer responsibility schemes attempt different scales of response.
now.open_questions: Can ocean cleanup work at scale? Most experts argue prevention upstream is far more effective than removal downstream.

items.reflection: Plastics were marketed in the 1950s as miracles. Disposable culture was an industry creation, not a consumer demand. The history of waste is the history of a manufactured behaviour.

moments.title: Cradle to Cradle published
moments.body: The book argues that products should be designed so that materials cycle indefinitely as either biological nutrients (compostable) or technical nutrients (recyclable). The book itself was printed on a plastic 'paper' that could be recycled into new books.
moments.takeaway: 'Reduce, reuse, recycle' as a hierarchy was supplemented by the more radical claim that waste should not exist in design.

moments.title: Ellen MacArthur Foundation founded
moments.body: After her solo circumnavigation record (2005), MacArthur retires from sailing to focus on circular economy. The Foundation works with major corporates (Unilever, Nike, Google, IKEA), governments and academics. Its definition of circular economy becomes widely adopted.
moments.takeaway: A round-the-world solo sailor became one of the most influential voices in industrial system design.

now.title: Circular economy today
now.body: EU's Circular Economy Action Plan (2020) and Right to Repair (2024) are major regulatory commitments. Extended Producer Responsibility schemes spread. Circular Gap Report (2024): only 7.2% of materials cycled. Critical minerals for the energy transition (lithium, cobalt, rare earths) are driving renewed interest in recycling.
now.open_questions: Can material flows really be decoupled from economic activity? Empirical evidence at economy-wide scale is limited.

items.reflection: MacArthur described seeing how isolated her boat was — a closed system with finite resources — as the genesis of her circular economy work. Sometimes a planetary metaphor needs a small-vessel scale to be felt.

moments.title: Lotka-Volterra equations
moments.body: Independently, Lotka (1925, 'Elements of Physical Biology') and Volterra (1926, observing Adriatic fish stocks) derive coupled differential equations for predator-prey dynamics. The equations produce oscillating populations — observed in lynx-hare data from the Hudson's Bay Company over 80+ years. Verhulst's earlier logistic equation (1838) for single populations had been forgotten and rediscovered.
moments.takeaway: Mathematical ecology emerged from two independent insights and was confirmed by century-old fur trapping records.

now.title: Population dynamics today
now.body: Lotka-Volterra is a teaching foundation but practical models are far more complex (age structure, stochasticity, spatial dynamics, climate forcing). Fishery management uses sophisticated stock-assessment models; many large fisheries have collapsed despite them. North Atlantic cod (1992 collapse) remains a cautionary case.
now.open_questions: Can ecosystem-based management replace single-species fishery models? Multi-species interactions are observable but hard to predict.

items.reflection: Volterra's daughter married a marine biologist whose Adriatic fish data prompted the modelling. Family conversations occasionally launch sub-fields.

moments.title: Limits to Growth
moments.who: Donella Meadows, Dennis Meadows, Jorgen Randers, William Behrens, MIT (Club of Rome)
moments.body: World3 — a system-dynamics model of population, food, industrial output, resources and pollution — projects 'standard run' overshoot and collapse in the 21st century. The book sells 30 million copies and is widely attacked for predicting near-term resource depletion. 30-year and 40-year updates (2004, 2012) and 2014 scientific reviews suggest the standard run is still roughly tracking.
moments.takeaway: An MIT computer model from 1972 produced a planetary forecast that has been one of the most influential — and most contested — projections in environmental science.

now.title: Earth system modelling today
now.body: Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs) combine economics and climate (DICE, FUND, PAGE). The IPCC uses them. Critics (Steve Keen, Nicholas Stern) argue IAMs underestimate climate damages. Planetary boundaries (Rockström 2009, updated 2023) extends the Limits framing.
now.open_questions: How well do current models capture non-linear collapse risks?

items.reflection: Donella Meadows continued writing about systems thinking until her death in 2001. Her 1999 essay 'Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System' is widely read in sustainability practice.

moments.title: Flint water crisis begins
moments.body: In April 2014, the city of Flint (majority Black, 41% below poverty line) switches its water source from Detroit to the Flint River as a cost-cutting measure under state-appointed emergency management. Corrosion control is not added. Lead from old pipes leaches into drinking water. Officials deny the problem for over a year. Marc Edwards (Virginia Tech) and Dr Mona Hanna-Attisha (paediatrician) document elevated blood lead levels in children.
moments.takeaway: Cost-cutting on a public utility produced a documented public health disaster in a majority-Black US city in 2014-15.

now.title: Lead in water today
now.body: EPA's Lead and Copper Rule revisions (2024) require replacement of all lead service lines within 10 years. Estimated 9 million US homes have lead pipes. Many other countries — UK, France, Canada — have similar legacies. Lead exposure remains a global environmental health issue.
now.open_questions: Will lead pipe replacement be funded at the required scale? The 2021 US infrastructure law allocated $15bn — less than needed.

items.reflection: Flint became a case study in environmental justice: which communities get clean water depends on race, income and political voice. Robert Bullard's 'Dumping in Dixie' (1990) had named this pattern 25 years earlier.

moments.title: Greta Thunberg's school strike
moments.body: On 20 August 2018, 15-year-old Greta Thunberg sits outside the Swedish parliament with a sign reading 'Skolstrejk för klimatet' (school strike for climate). The protest spreads. Fridays for Future becomes a global movement. The 20 September 2019 global climate strike draws an estimated 4 million participants in 161 countries.

quote.text: I want you to act as if the house is on fire. Because it is.

moments.takeaway: A teenager sitting alone outside parliament with a sign generated the largest environmental protest movement in history within 14 months.

now.title: Climate activism today
now.body: Extinction Rebellion (founded 2018) uses civil disobedience. Last Generation, Just Stop Oil, and similar groups extend confrontational tactics. Youth-led climate litigation (Held v. Montana 2023, Duarte Agostinho v. 32 states ECHR 2024) is producing legal precedent. Public protest fatigue and policing pushback are real factors.
now.open_questions: How do protest movements convert visibility into policy?

items.reflection: Thunberg sailed across the Atlantic in 2019 to avoid flying. The symbolism worked — and was widely mocked. Movement-building requires both symbolic action and theory of change.

moments.title: Minamata disease identified
moments.body: From 1932, Chisso's chemical plant discharges methylmercury into Minamata Bay. The compound bioaccumulates in fish. From 1956 (and earlier in cats and seabirds), local people develop severe neurological symptoms — Minamata disease. Chisso continues discharging mercury until 1968. By 2001, 2,265 victims are officially certified; the true number is much higher.
moments.takeaway: Industrial bioaccumulative pollution caused multi-generational neurological damage in a Japanese fishing community. The company knew of the problem and continued.

moments.title: Minamata Convention on Mercury
moments.body: The Minamata Convention is adopted on 10 October 2013, named for the city. It aims to reduce mercury emissions, ban new mercury mines, and phase out mercury use in many products (batteries, switches, dental amalgam over time). Enters into force 2017.
moments.takeaway: A treaty named for a pollution disaster became the framework for global mercury regulation 57 years after the disease was identified.

now.title: Heavy metals today
now.body: Mercury emissions are decreasing in OECD countries; artisanal small-scale gold mining remains a major source in low-income countries. Eugene Smith's photograph 'Tomoko Uemura in Her Bath' (1971) of a Minamata victim — withdrawn from publication at her family's request — remains one of the iconic images of environmental injustice.
now.open_questions: Can mercury emissions from artisanal gold mining be reduced without harming livelihoods? Sustainable gold initiatives have limited reach.

items.reflection: Chisso paid compensation in 1973, 41 years after the discharges began. Justice in environmental disasters tends to be partial and very late.

moments.title: Acid rain politics
moments.body: Sweden submits the first major paper on acid rain to the 1972 Stockholm Conference. Scandinavian forests and lakes acidify from UK and German emissions. Canada-US disputes over US Midwest power plants drive 'transboundary pollution' into policy vocabulary. The US 1990 Clean Air Act amendments introduce SO₂ cap-and-trade — a successful market mechanism that becomes a climate-policy template.
moments.takeaway: Acid rain was solved through international diplomacy, scientific assessment, and market-based regulation within ~20 years. It was a precursor to climate negotiations.

now.title: Atmospheric pollution today
now.body: SO₂ emissions in OECD countries are down ~80% from peak. Coal scrubbers and natural gas substitution did most of the work. Acid rain damage to forests has substantially reversed in much of Europe and North America. China's SO₂ emissions peaked around 2007 and have declined sharply.
now.open_questions: Has acid rain returned as climate policy reduces sulphate aerosols? Marine sulphur reductions (IMO 2020 ship fuel rules) may slightly warm the climate by removing cooling aerosols.

items.reflection: Acid rain is often forgotten as 'solved' but it serves as a useful counterexample to fatalistic environmental narratives. International cooperation, regulation and technology change can together solve a major environmental problem within a generation.

moments.title: Amazon under Bolsonaro
moments.body: Annual Amazon deforestation more than doubles under President Jair Bolsonaro (2019-22), reaching 13,038 km² in 2021. Indigenous land invasions, illegal mining and ranching surge. Global attention is highest in August 2019 when fires fill the skies of São Paulo with smoke. International donor countries (Norway, Germany) freeze Amazon Fund payments.
moments.takeaway: National political shifts can rapidly increase deforestation. Decades of progress reversed in years.

moments.title: Lula's deforestation crackdown
moments.body: Under Lula's third presidency, Amazon deforestation falls 50% in 2023 (Brazilian Amazon, PRODES data). Indigenous Affairs Ministry (MPI) is created. Funai's authority is restored. The Belém Declaration (2023) signed by 8 Amazon nations seeks regional coordination.
moments.takeaway: Deforestation rates fell almost as fast as they had risen, with a new government and the same satellite data.

now.title: Amazon today
now.body: Recent research (Gatti et al. 2021) suggests the southeastern Amazon is already a net carbon source. Drought years (2023-24, severe) accelerate tree mortality. Indigenous territories continue to have lower deforestation than other forest categories — empirically supporting indigenous-led conservation.
now.open_questions: Has the Amazon already passed the tipping point in some regions? Atmospheric and rainfall feedbacks are difficult to reverse once triggered.

items.reflection: Brazilian satellites (CBERS series, jointly with China) and INPE's PRODES monitoring give Brazil ground truth its own government cannot dispute. Open data and independent monitoring matter for political accountability.

moments.title: Global Plastics Treaty negotiations
moments.body: On 2 March 2022, UNEA-5.2 in Nairobi mandates negotiation of a legally binding instrument on plastic pollution. The Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC) meets five times (Punta del Este 2022, Paris 2023, Nairobi 2023, Ottawa 2024, Busan 2024). Major dispute: cap plastic production (high-ambition coalition) vs focus on waste management (oil-producing states).
moments.takeaway: The architecture of a global plastics treaty is being negotiated now. Whether it caps production or only manages waste will shape the next 50 years.

now.title: Plastics today
now.body: Annual plastic production: ~450 million tonnes, doubling roughly every 20 years. ~10% recycled. EU Single-Use Plastics Directive (2019) banned cotton buds, cutlery, plates, straws, balloon sticks and EPS containers. Microplastics are now detected in placenta, breast milk and lung tissue.
now.open_questions: Can the treaty cover the full life cycle of plastics including production? Saudi Arabia, Iran, Russia, China are major opponents.

items.reflection: Plastic was marketed as a miracle material in the 1950s by industry. The petrochemical companies producing it 70 years later are the leading opponents of a production cap. Industry incumbents oppose what they once invented.

moments.title: A Sand County Almanac
moments.body: Published a year after Leopold's death (1948, fighting a neighbour's grass fire), Sand County Almanac includes 'The Land Ethic': 'A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community. It is wrong when it tends otherwise.' Leopold's earlier essay 'Thinking Like a Mountain' describes the wolf's death he caused as a young Forest Service official.

quote.text: Conservation is a state of harmony between men and land.

moments.takeaway: A US Forest Service official's gradual evolution from predator-control hunter to ecological philosopher produced the foundational ethical text of American environmentalism.

now.title: Environmental ethics today
now.body: Leopold's land ethic, Naess's deep ecology (1973), Singer's animal liberation (1975), and Hardin's tragedy of the commons (1968 — though now critically read) form a 20th-century philosophical canon. Rights of nature (Ecuador 2008 constitution, Whanganui River 2017) embeds environmental ethics in law.
now.open_questions: Can rights of nature work as legal infrastructure? Standing, enforcement and conflict with development rights are real questions.

items.reflection: Leopold shot a wolf in 1909 and watched 'a fierce green fire dying in her eyes'. The essay he wrote 30 years later — never published in his lifetime — became one of the most-quoted environmental texts. Slow change inside one person can outlive them.

moments.title: Serageldin warning
moments.body: World Bank Vice-President Ismail Serageldin warns 'the wars of the next century will be fought over water'. Actual record: many transboundary water disputes are managed (Indus Waters Treaty 1960, Nile Basin Initiative, Mekong Commission). But Cape Town's 'Day Zero' (2018), Iran's water crisis (2021-), Yemen's collapse, and Israeli-Palestinian water disputes all show stress.
moments.takeaway: Water-driven international conflict has been rarer than 1990s warnings suggested — partly because diplomacy worked, partly because the worst conflicts are within rather than between states.

now.title: Water today
now.body: UN World Water Development Report estimates 2.2 billion lack safely managed drinking water. Climate change is shifting precipitation patterns. India's groundwater depletion (NASA GRACE data) is among the world's fastest. Cape Town avoided Day Zero (2018) through emergency rationing.
now.open_questions: Can transboundary water cooperation hold as climate stress intensifies? Indus Waters Treaty has been suspended by India following 2019, 2025 tensions.

items.reflection: Water management at urban scale is one of civilisation's oldest activities — Roman aqueducts, Iranian qanats, Mesopotamian irrigation. Modern megacities have not yet faced sustained drought of the kind that brought down some earlier civilisations.

moments.title: Carbon markets and scandals
moments.who: Kyoto Protocol mechanisms, voluntary carbon markets
moments.body: Kyoto introduces emissions trading, the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) and Joint Implementation. The EU ETS (2005-) becomes the largest cap-and-trade system. Voluntary carbon markets grow rapidly post-2015. Investigations by The Guardian, Die Zeit and SourceMaterial (2023) find ~90% of Verra rainforest credits are likely 'phantom' — not delivering real emissions reductions.
moments.takeaway: Carbon markets, in principle a price-discovery mechanism for climate action, have struggled with measurement, verification and corporate greenwashing in practice.

now.title: Carbon markets today
now.body: EU ETS prices reached €90+/tonne in 2023, providing real abatement incentive in covered sectors. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement (rules finalised at COP26 Glasgow, 2021) governs new international transfers. Voluntary markets have shrunk after credibility concerns. Carbon removal (CDR) credits — direct air capture, biochar, enhanced weathering — are emerging.
now.open_questions: Can carbon markets be made credible enough to deliver climate outcomes? Or are direct regulation and standards more reliable?

items.reflection: The price of carbon — what climate damage costs per tonne — has been studied for 30 years. Estimates range from $50 to $1000+ per tonne. The political price (the EU ETS price) has been a fraction of the social cost. Markets reveal more about preferences than about damages.
